newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident blames Beijing boss for crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China dissident blames Beijing boss for crackdown.

text.p: A Chinese dissident on Tuesday issued a daring call for disgraced Beijing leader Chen Xitong to be brought to justice, blaming him for a 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protests.

In an open letter to the leader of China's National People's Congress, or parliament, veteran dissident Jin Cheng said residents of the capital were still awaiting a public accounting for Chen's actions as city leader.
Chen has been out of the public eye since he was toppled from his posts as Beijing Communist Party secretary and member of the elite party Politburo during a huge corruption scandal in 1995.

The former leader should be held responsible for his part in the scandal and for his role in the crushing of student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing on June 4, 1989, wrote Jin in his letter, a copy of which was given to Reuters.
Chen had misrepresented the motives and goals of the demonstrators, prompting leaders to order the bloody army assault, wrote the 38-year-old activist and former official.
"For his own ulterior motives, Chen Xitong fabricated stories, deceived his superiors, deluded his subordinates and made false reports to the central leaders," he wrote.
"Before this, central leaders had no intention of using extreme measures... so Chen Xitong should take inescapable responsibility for the tragedy," he wrote.

Whether to review the 1989 killing of hundreds of protesters and Beijing residents remains one of the most sensitive issues facing China's leaders, who will in September or October hold a congress to appoint leaders and fix policy for the next five years.

The death last February of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who publicly backed the crackdown, was widely seen as an opportunity for Beijing to alter its judgment that tough action was needed in 1989 to end a counter-revolutionary rebellion.
Analysts have said top leaders are unlikely to rethink their stand on the crackdown in the near future, despite calls from dissidents and private pressure from some officials,

Aside from his role in the crushing of the Tiananmen Square democracy demonstrations, Chen should be publicly tried for corruption and abuse of power, wrote Jin, who was jailed for publishing an underground magazine after the 1989 crackdown.
Rampant corruption in official ranks would spread further if the legal system was not seen to be able to bring to justice even those with political influence, he wrote.

A senior Beijing official said last February that Chen, whose name has become a byword for graft in the Chinese capital, could be punished for dereliction of duty but would not be charged with any more serious offence.
"Beijing residents are very concerned by this case but in the last two years it has not been cleared up," Jin told Reuters.
Appeals and petitions to the communist-led government that touch on sensitive issues are risky political acts in China, which has clamped down hard on dissent in recent years.
Jin said he was not concerned about the consequences of his move.
"I am not afraid," said the activist, who was dismissed from his post after his release from prison in 1993 and who has since been subject to surveillance and occasional detention.
"Fear is China's tragedy," he said. "If everyone is afraid, there is no hope."
